title: A Buddha on the shelf
hook: a Buddha head in a garden center, a bar, a tattoo: why many Buddhists care how the image is used, and why customs differ (SN 22.87)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the butsudan, the home shrine: an image, a candle, incense, a flower, water, kept high and clean. Your line was a quiet corner. Day one hundred forty.

A stone Buddha head in a garden center, between the gnomes and the birdbaths. A golden Buddha behind the bar of a lounge, lit purple. A small seated Buddha tattooed on an ankle. Show those to a room of Buddhists and you'll get very different answers. Some will wince. Some will shrug and say he meets people where they are. Both answers come from people who love the Buddha. Today: why the image matters, and why the customs aren't the same everywhere.
screen: `A BUDDHA HEAD BY THE GNOMES.` → `A BUDDHA BEHIND THE BAR.` → `WINCE, OR SHRUG?`

segments.voice: An image of the Buddha is called a buddharupa: a Buddha form. Yesterday's customs, high and clean, come from a simple idea that runs through much of Asia. The head is the most honored part of the body, and the feet the lowest. So an image goes up high. Not on the floor, not in a bathroom, not where feet will point at it. That's why a Buddha on a barroom shelf, or on an ankle, can sting. A head alone can sting too: for many people it calls to mind temple statues broken up and sold. Some countries limit taking Buddha images abroad, and some temples post signs asking visitors not to treat the Buddha as decoration. Elsewhere, the customs are looser. Many Buddhists in the West keep an image on a bookshelf or a desk, and plenty of teachers say any image that reminds you to be kind is doing its job. There's an old story that holds both sides. A monk named Vakkali loved to gaze at the Buddha's body, and could hardly do anything else. The Buddha told him, in effect: why look at this body, which will decay? Whoever sees the teaching sees me. So the image points past itself. It isn't a god, and it isn't decor. It's a reminder, and people treat it with the care you'd give a photo of someone you love. Customs differ by country, and nobody here is checking your shelves. If you keep one, give it a clean, high place, and you'll rarely go wrong.
screen: `BUDDHARUPA — A BUDDHA FORM.` · `THE HEAD HIGH, THE FEET LOW.` · `WHY A HEAD ALONE CAN STING.` · `WHO SEES THE TEACHING SEES ME.` · then, large: `CUSTOMS DIFFER, CARE DOESN'T.`

segments.voice: Settle and breathe. Picture a Buddha image you've seen somewhere: a statue, a poster, a garden, a temple. Notice your first reaction, whatever it is, without arguing with it. Then let the image do what it was made for. Let it remind you of something: stillness, kindness, a person who woke up. Rest with that, and let the image fade while the reminder stays. The bell holds the time.
Buddharupa. A Buddha form: an image of the Buddha, kept high and clean in many homes, a reminder that points past itself. Today's word.
Your line: customs differ, care doesn't. The shelf can change from country to country; the respect travels with you. Day one hundred forty.

howItsDone: In many Buddhist homes and temples, the Buddha image sits high and clean, above head height when people are seated, never on the floor or near shoes; customs about decor and tattoos vary by country and community.

fork.setup: a friend gives you a small Buddha statue as a housewarming gift. you have a bookshelf, a coffee table, and the spot by the door where the shoes pile up. where does it go?
options: by the door, to greet guests.
on top of the bookshelf, kept clean.

fork.reveal: in many Buddhist homes: high and clean, never near the shoes. a shelf you see every day is a fine place.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit: Buddha-form, an image of the Buddha (rupa, form).

trapdoor: what you thought: a Buddha statue is either decor or an idol.
what it means: a reminder, treated with care, whose customs differ by country.

what a scholar hears: SN 22.87 (Vakkali): 'one who sees the dhamma sees me'; the earliest surviving Buddhist art often shows him by symbols, a footprint, a wheel, an empty seat, and scholars still debate why.

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 22.87 (Vakkali Sutta): whoever sees the dhamma sees me
